title: Highly integrated quantum key distribution transmitter enabled by silicon photonics
authors: Rende Liu, Yan-Lin Tang, Cheng-Guang Dong, Yan Ma, Guo-Qing Liu, Zhi-Lin Xie, Shuai Li, Mi Zou, Hao Liang, Shi-biao Tang
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) provides information-theoretic security independent of computational assumptions, yet the bulk and cost of current systems hinder large-scale deployment. Although integrated photonic technologies have enabled highly integrated QKD chips, practical QKD transmitters are still predominantly implemented as rack-mounted systems. Here, we demonstrate a highly integrated standalone QKD transmitter that integrates all essential functionalities required for practical QKD operation within a compact platform built around a silicon photonic encoding chip. The transmitter occupies only $167 \times 56 \times 21~\mathrm{mm}^3$ ($\sim 0.2~\mathrm{dm}^3$), comparable in size to a half-height, half-width PCIe card and more than 30 times smaller in volume than a conventional 1U rack-mounted system. Paired with a conventional discrete-component receiver, it achieves a secure key rate of 219.1 kbps over 51.3 km of standard single-mode fiber, with performance comparable to that of conventional discrete-component implementations. This work bridges the gap between photonic chip integration and deployable QKD hardware, marking an important step toward transitioning QKD transmitters from conventional rack-mounted equipment to compact board-level platforms.
summary: This paper presents a novel, highly integrated standalone transmitter for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) that overcomes the bulk limitations of current rack-mounted systems. By combining monolithic silicon photonics with an embedded System-on-Chip, they achieved practical key rates over tens of kilometers in a dramatically reduced physical footprint. This work marks a significant engineering milestone toward commercializing compact QKD hardware.
main_problem: The large size, cost, and complexity of current Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) hardware hinder its widespread deployment.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a highly integrated, standalone QKD transmitter that achieves practical key rates comparable to conventional systems while being significantly smaller than rack-mounted equipment.
method: They employed a hybrid integration strategy combining monolithic silicon photonics for quantum state preparation with an external programmable System-on-Chip (SoC) for real-time protocol execution and control.
model_or_system: The system is a standalone QKD transmitter built around a silicon photonic encoding chip, integrating components like DFB lasers, MEMS-VOA, and the entire BB84 post-processing chain onto a compact board-level platform.
key_observables: Secure key rate (SKR) of 219.1 kbps over 51.3 km; stable operation maintained over continuous 12-hour tests.
important_parameters: Transmitter volume: $167 	imes 56 	imes 21 	ext{ mm}^3$ ($\sim 0.2 	ext{ dm}^3$), representing a reduction of $>30	imes$ compared to 1U rack systems.
main_assumptions: The reported key rates are considered conservative as they assume a deployment-oriented receiver architecture, which differs from ideal laboratory setups.
figures_summary: Figures show photographs and schematics of the integrated transmitter, block diagrams detailing optical and electronic subsystems, and plots illustrating SKR vs. distance and QBER stability over time.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of QKD deployment limitations, details the hybrid architecture integrating photonics (SiPh) and electronics (SoC), presents performance measurements (key rates/stability), and concludes by positioning this work as a major step toward compact, deployable hardware.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and photonic QI as it tackles the engineering challenge of scaling up quantum communication protocols from lab benches to field-deployable devices using advanced silicon photonics integration techniques.
